region: Europe; the related American beech (Fagus grandifolia) grows in eastern North America
description: European beech is a pale, hard, close-grained hardwood used for furniture, chairs, workbenches, tool handles, turnery and veneer. It steams and bends well, and is often sold steamed to a pinkish tone. American beech is a close relative used in similar ways.

hazards.summary: Workers with nasal allergy to European beech dust have been confirmed by specific provocation testing and case reports. In Danish furniture workers about 3% had IgE antibodies to beech, though this was mostly not linked to symptoms.
UK HSE lists reduced lung function for beech. A French study of beech and oak furniture workers found more sore throat and twitchy airways as dust levels rose.
UK HSE lists dermatitis among the reported effects of beech. The mechanism (irritant or allergic) is not specified.
UK HSE lists eye irritation for beech and notes that lichens growing on the bark may be responsible.
IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long, heavy exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.
ACGIH names beech dust specifically as a confirmed human carcinogen (A1), the same class it gives oak.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour TWA; ACGIH value as restated by OSHA.

related_species_note: Clinical evidence here comes from European beech (Fagus sylvatica). No species-specific reports for American beech (Fagus grandifolia) were found; ACGIH's A1 listing says only 'beech'. Treat American beech dust with the same precautions. One study found no cross-reactivity between beech wood and beech pollen (Kespohl-2010).
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed European beech (Fagus sylvatica) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Even pale pinkish-tan to light biscuit color across the whole face, with little difference between heartwood and sapwood. Straight, fine, even texture with tiny diffuse pores; small, dense reddish-brown ray flecks scattered across the surface like short dashes, a soft satin luster. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of European beech with even pale pinkish-tan color and fine scattered ray flecks.
notes_internal: Hernandez-1999 is a letter with no abstract; methods unread. Spiewak 1994 (Ann Agric Environ Med 1;73-76, ash/oak/beech/pine asthma case) has no PMID and was not cited; see verify file. Bohadana-2000 mixes beech and oak workers. HSE-WIS30 parenthetical 'possibly from bark lichens' sits after 'eye irritation' and may apply to all listed effects; attached only to eye irritation here. Asthma (as opposed to rhinitis) from beech is not supported here by a verified primary with provocation testing.
